answers.question: Which experiments tested above 30% oxygen?
answers.answer: The sources show that ACME BRE tested in an atmosphere of about 30% oxygen [5]. ACME s-Flame tested at approximately 30% oxygen with nitrogen and helium atmospheres [2][3][4]. ACME CFI-G tested at approximately 40% oxygen [6][7]. ACME Flame Design tested oxygen from 19.8 to 40% in surrounding air and 21.2 to 85% oxygen flowing out of the burner for inverse flames [1]. FLEX tested oxygen from 12 to 34% [1]. ACME CFI-G tested oxygen from 18 to 40% [1]. ACME BRE tested oxygen from 21 to 40% [1]. ACME s-Flame tested oxygen from 21 to 30% [1].

answers.question: Is there fire data in Moon gravity?
answers.answer: Yes. The LUCI project achieved the first-ever extended duration combustion tests greater than 25 seconds in simulated Lunar gravity [1]. The FM2 experiment will conduct the first-ever observations and measurements of flame spread on the Moon at its 1/6 reduced gravity level [2]. FM2 will verify whether some materials burning in partial-gravity environments may be more flammable compared to 1g [3]. The sources do not cover fire data from actual Moon surface conditions yet, as FM2 is planned to launch in late 2026 [4].

answers.question: What did SAME find about the station's smoke detectors?
answers.answer: The ISS smoke detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the SAME tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of the tests [6]. It also does not select for smoke particles, so suspended dust can cause nuisance alarms [6]. SAME results show that substantial portions of smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter and that mixing dominates smoke transport, leading to longer detection time lags than in normal gravity [2].

answers.question: Did NASA invent the smoke detector?
answers.answer: No, NASA did not invent the smoke detector. Ionization detectors were becoming broadly available for home use in the 1970s, and the Space Shuttle used the most advanced detection technology available at that time [2]. The ISS forward light scattering detector utilized improvements in photodiode technology developed in the 1990s [2]. The sources do not cover who invented the smoke detector.

answers.question: How does BASS-II compare to BASS?
answers.answer: BASS ran from 2012 to 2013 with 122 tests, while BASS-II ran from 2014 to 2018 with 129 tests [1]. BASS-II tested oxygen levels from 13.6 to 22.2 percent [1]. The sources do not provide a direct comparison of results between BASS and BASS-II.

answers.question: How do FLEX and FLEX-2 differ?
answers.answer: FLEX studies droplet combustion to improve chemical kinetic models and evaluate inert gas flame extinguishment for spacecraft safety [1][5]. FLEX-2 is the follow-on experiment and uses fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions [1]. It studies sub-buoyant convective flows on combustion rates, the influence of a second burning droplet on a linear array, and practical fuels such as bi-component and surrogate fuels [1]. FLEX-2 also continues to examine steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena, flame extinction, soot formation mechanisms, and radiative heat transfer [5]. It uses the MDCA insert in the CIR with the same diagnostic packages plus a second HiBMS camera [1].

answers.question: How did FLEX test fire suppressants?
answers.answer: FLEX tested fire suppressants by burning liquid fuel droplets in microgravity aboard the ISS from 2009 to 2011 [1]. The chamber was filled with various concentrations of suppressants or suppressant blends along with enough oxygen to support a flame [5]. Droplet extinction diameters and droplet regression rates were used as figures of merit to compare suppressant effectiveness [5]. Tests covered oxygen levels from 12 to 34 percent and pressures from 0.69 to 3.05 atmospheres using methanol and heptane fuels [1]. The sources do not state how suppressants were delivered or which specific suppressants were tested.

answers.question: Which studies measured smoke particles?
answers.answer: SAME-2 measured smoke particles by collecting samples on Transmission Electron Microscope grids and analyzing particle morphology and size parameters [2]. It used moment diagnostics to determine particle number concentration, diameter concentration, and mass concentration, then calculated count mean diameter, diameter of average mass, geometric mean diameter, and geometric standard deviation [2]. SAME-R also collected smoke particle samples on TEM grids for post-flight analysis and measured particle morphology and size parameters using the same moment diagnostics [3]. SAME was the first study to examine oxidative pyrolysis particles in microgravity [5].

answers.question: What did SPICE measure?
answers.answer: SPICE measured laminar smoke points in non-buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station [2]. It found fifty-two smoke points for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures [2]. SPICE also measured overall flame shape, flame stabilization heights, and temperature field [1]. The sources do not state what specific instruments were used to make these measurements.

answers.question: Why are flames round and blue in space?
answers.answer: In microgravity, buoyant gravity-driven flow is absent, so flames take a spherical shape [5]. The blue color comes from chemiluminescence of the excited CH molecule, which emits blue 431-nm light [4]. The sources do not explain why flames are round and blue together as a combined phenomenon.

answers.question: What is a cool flame?
answers.answer: A cool flame is a low-temperature combustion regime marked by very weak but sustained burning [6]. It appears after hot flames radiatively extinguish, with no visible luminosity for about one second before becoming evident [1]. Cool flames are dimmer and smaller than hot flames, and their reaction intensity gradually decreases from the peak outward rather than forming a sharp flame sheet [1]. Cool flame extinction is controlled primarily by chemical kinetics [4].

answers.question: What is the smoke point?
answers.answer: The smoke point is the condition and luminous flame length where a flame begins to emit soot. It indicates the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames and represents the properties of the largest laminar jet diffusion flames that do not emit soot [3][5]. The SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non-buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station [3].

answers.question: How did space research lead to lighter firefighter air tanks?
answers.answer: NASA-Johnson developed breathing equipment concepts and hardware for astronauts working outside spacecraft or on the moon [1]. Through a NASA-sponsored program, Scott Aviation created a lighter firefighter air tank based on that work [2]. The new backpack system weighed 20 pounds for a 30-minute air supply, 13 pounds less than conventional tanks, and was pressurized at 4,500 psi, about twice the pressure of current tanks [1][2]. It used an aluminum liner wrapped by resin-impregnated glass fibers, which eliminated corrosion and lightened the load [1][2]. The harness shifted most of the weight from the shoulders to the hips [1][2].

answers.question: What replaced the station's CO₂ fire extinguishers?
answers.answer: Fine-water-mist portable fire extinguishers replaced the station's CO₂ fire extinguishers [3][5][6]. A set of nine fine-water-mist extinguishers were built to replace the carbon dioxide extinguishers that were incompatible with astronaut emergency breathing equipment [5][6]. The first two were sent to the ISS in December 2015, and the rest arrived in three more missions [3].

answers.question: What did BASS find?
answers.answer: BASS completed 115 burns on 41 solid samples aboard the International Space Station [2]. It measured flame appearance, behavior, spread rate, and extinction dynamics while varying airflow speed up to 40 cm/s in opposed and concurrent flow [2][3]. The results improve material fire safety rating tests, guide fire detection and suppression strategies in microgravity, and validate combustion models [5]. BASS tested the hypothesis that materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation burn as well if not better than in normal gravity [6].

answers.question: Why did the rod burn at lower oxygen in space?
answers.answer: In microgravity, buoyant flow is eliminated, so convective cooling of the rod is lower and heat losses are reduced. Gas-phase radiative feedback becomes an important heat transfer process that extends the flammability limit to lower oxygen concentrations. BASS-II obtained steady spreading at 13.6% oxygen for the ¼-inch PMMA rod, compared with a 1g blowoff at 16% oxygen [5][4]. Microgravity flames can burn at as much as 2-3 percent less oxygen than under normal gravity [6].

answers.question: How does airflow change flame spread in space?
answers.answer: In microgravity, buoyant flow is eliminated, so forced airflow controls flame spread direction and rate. BASS-II tests used airflow speeds from 0 to 55 cm/s in opposed and concurrent flow configurations [2][7]. For thin PMMA sheets, spread rate remains relatively independent of opposing airflow velocity until it reaches 40 cm/s [3]. At low forced-flow velocities in space, flames spread upstream into the oncoming airflow, unlike normal gravity where flames spread downstream in the buoyant flow direction even without forced flow [5]. Concurrent-flow tests with PMMA rods showed flames surviving at airflow less than 1 cm/s [6]. The sources do not state the exact quantitative relationship between airflow speed and flame spread rate across all tested materials and conditions.

answers.answer: The sources say that materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation may burn more readily compared to normal gravity when other conditions are identical [3]. The sources do not provide a definitive conclusion that materials burn more readily in space than on Earth.

answers.answer: SPICE measured smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air, emphasizing small burners and the effects of coflow velocity [2]. The sources do not state the specific numerical smoke point results or which fuels produced which smoke points.

answers.question: What did FLEX find?
answers.answer: FLEX found that droplets continued to vaporize vigorously after visible flame extinction, sustained by a low-temperature, soot-free chemical reaction called cool flame [4]. This phenomenon was not explained by conventional droplet combustion theories and represented a new chemistry different from hot combustion [4]. Cool flames could persist after hot-flame extinction and possibly reignite in hot mode, indicating increased fire risk in microgravity habitats and the need for more rigorous suppression [4]. FLEX also obtained droplet and flame diameter histories, burning-rate constants, and extinction diameters for methanol and n-heptane droplets [7].

answers.question: What did ACME BRE find?
answers.answer: The ACME BRE study found that steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm diameter in microgravity [3][4]. Flames generally persisted for 2 minutes or more at atmospheric conditions of 27% oxygen and 10.2 psia, and at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psia [3]. Solid materials with heats of combustion in the range 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heats of gasification from about 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn in microgravity [2]. Lower pressure and higher oxygen concentration favor long duration burning [2].

answers.question: What did ACME CLD Flame find?
answers.answer: ACME CLD Flame found that microgravity flames contain five to eight times more soot than equivalent normal-gravity flames [2]. Microgravity flames are taller and wider [2]. Microgravity increases the limits of fuel dilution for both methane and ethylene flames [2]. Near limits, microgravity flames are more stable, allowing for lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations [2]. Early results show that dilution limits are extended in microgravity compared to normal gravity [5]. Steady microgravity flames are more stable and have lower lift-off heights due to the lack of buoyancy [5].

answers.question: What did ACME E-FIELD Flames find?
answers.answer: The ACME E-FIELD Flames study found that high-voltage electric fields create forces similar to buoyancy, which dramatically affected flame shape, intensity, and soot production [1]. The ion-driven wind from charged ions produced by combustion influences flame stability and sooting behavior [1][2]. Tests were conducted in microgravity to simplify analysis and develop more efficient, less polluting combustion technology for Earth [1][2]. The sources do not provide specific quantitative findings for E-FIELD Flames beyond these qualitative results.

answers.question: What did ACME s-Flame find?
answers.answer: ACME s-Flame advanced the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames [2][3]. With helium dilution instead of nitrogen, extinction limits shifted and kinetic extinction became generally difficult to discern [5]. The results may contribute to lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions on Earth [2]. The sources do not state specific quantitative findings from the s-Flame tests.

answers.question: What did ACME Flame Design find?
answers.answer: ACME Flame Design studied soot production and control to optimize oxygen-enriched combustion and design robust, soot-free flames [5]. Flame size increases with reactant flow rate and decreases with ambient oxygen concentration [5]. Very small flames have low soot [5]. Soot can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, so this may lead to more efficient and cleaner burner designs [2]. The sources do not provide the complete list of all findings.

answers.question: What did ACME CFI-G find?
answers.answer: ACME CFI-G observed 280 hot diffusion flames, of which 189 experienced radiative extinction and 15 subsequently reignited as cool diffusion flames [3]. Cool flames were found only with 30 vol% n-butane and 40 vol% O2, normal flames, and a pressure of 2.03 bar [3]. They give off little heat or light and were revealed by thermal radiation and burner temperature measurements after hot flames quenched [5]. The sources do not state the overall conclusion of the study.

answers.question: What did Saffire-I find?
answers.answer: Saffire-I showed that steady flame spread over a large thin charring surface was possible in low gravity, unlike normal gravity [3]. Concurrent flame spread with the wind was more sensitive to flow duct dimensions than previously anticipated [3]. Large-scale experiments could be safely conducted in an unmanned spacecraft [3]. The sources do not state the specific burn time or other quantitative results for Saffire-I.

answers.question: What did Saffire-II find?
answers.answer: The sources do not report specific findings from Saffire-II. Source [6] states that the objective of Saffire-II was to quantify how low-gravity affects flammability limits using samples the same size as those used in normal-gravity tests, with some samples expected to burn and others not. Source [3] lists results for Saffire-I through III collectively, including that steady flame spread over a large thin charring surface was possible in low-gravity, concurrent flame spread was more sensitive to flow duct dimension than anticipated, and large-scale experiments could be safely conducted in an unmanned spacecraft. The sources do not separate Saffire-II-specific findings from the combined results.

answers.question: What did SAME find?
answers.answer: SAME found that for the materials tested, a substantial portion of smoke particles were below 500 nm in diameter [4]. It also found that smoke transport in microgravity is dominated by mixing, causing longer detection time lags than in normal gravity [4]. The knowledge gained can be used to establish design requirements for smoke detectors on future spacecraft [4]. SAME-2 also demonstrated that a two-moment smoke detector could predict smoke number and mass concentration from its output [6].

answers.question: What did DAFT find?
answers.answer: DAFT found that overall particulate levels in the US Lab atmosphere were very low, about a factor of ten leaner than normal US office conditions [2]. It also found that the P-Trak responded well to Velcro dust, with several readings above 30,000 particles per cubic centimeter [2]. The experiment adequately demonstrated the reliability of the modified P-Trak as operated in low gravity [3].
